summary: Describes an architecture for DDoS Open Threat Signaling within and between domains. It does not specify protocols and instead defines the relationships, components and concepts of a DOTS deployment.

plainLanguage.summary: A plan showing who calls whom for help when a network gets flooded, without the details of the phone line.

subtitle: The big-picture design for letting a DDoS victim ask upstream networks for help, without specifying the protocols themselves.

tldr.problem: Defending against a distributed denial-of-service attack often needs help from other networks, but the parties need a shared understanding of roles and relationships to coordinate quickly.
tldr.mechanism: DOTS defines DOTS clients, servers and gateways that talk over a signal channel (for urgent mitigation requests) and a data channel (for configuration such as filters and aliases). A client asks, the server may pass the request to a mitigator, and status flows back.
tldr.outcome: The document specifies no protocol. It describes components, session handling, signaling modes and ways a mitigation request can be triggered, and it relies on the DOTS signal channel and data channel protocols for the wire details.

sections.title: The Basic DOTS Architecture
sections.content:
The basic picture has four parts: an attack target, a DOTS client near the target, a DOTS server upstream and a mitigator that the server invokes. The client signals for help, and the mitigator tries to suppress attack traffic while letting valid traffic through.

The scope of DOTS is only the interface between client and server. How a target decides it is under attack, and how a mitigator actually mitigates, are out of scope. A client's request is advisory and might not lead to any mitigation at all.

There are two interfaces between client and server. The signal channel carries mitigation requests, status and heartbeats, and must work even on a link saturated by attack traffic. The optional data channel carries configuration and policy such as aliases for resources, drop-lists, accept-lists and filters. It requires reliable delivery, so it is expected to be used mainly under normal conditions.
sections.plainLanguage: A shop being swamped by a crowd rings a security company (the server). The company sends guards (the mitigator) to sort real customers from troublemakers. The shop can also leave a list of friends to always let in.

sections.title: Clients, Servers and Gateways
sections.content:
A DOTS client is where requests originate. It sends heartbeats, can adjust the mitigation scope and may give feedback such as efficacy. A DOTS server receives and may act on requests. It authenticates and authorizes clients, tracks mitigations and reports their status. A server MUST reject mitigation requests, filtering rules and aliases for resources that the requesting client's domain does not own, and if it refuses a request it MUST include the reason in the server signal.

A DOTS gateway is a server and a client joined back to back, comparable to a SIP Back-to-Back User Agent. It looks like a server to downstream agents and a client to upstream ones, and it MUST fully terminate and reoriginate DOTS sessions. A gateway can aggregate several clients, or translate between TCP and UDP for the signal channel.

One server can serve many clients, and one client can use several servers. A multihomed client needs care: if it asks several uncoordinated servers to mitigate at once, the result could be a permanent routing loop as each mitigator tries to divert the same traffic. The RFC suggests requesting mitigation serially, dividing protected resources among servers, or restricting multihoming to servers that share mitigation resources.
sections.plainLanguage: The client is the one calling for help, the server is the one answering, and a gateway is a person in the middle who passes messages along. If you call three helpers who do not talk to each other, they might all start doing the same job and get in each other's way.

sections.title: DOTS Sessions and Heartbeats
sections.content:
A DOTS session carries data between a client and a server. It can be a signal channel session, a data channel session or both, and the server ties them together using the client's identity. A signal channel session uses one transport connection (TCP or UDP) and one security association (TLS or DTLS). A data channel session uses TCP and TLS. Mitigation requests belong to the client, not to a particular signal session.

Before a session starts, the parties are assumed to have agreed terms and the client is assumed to hold what it needs to reach the server, including cryptographic material. The client may then open the signal channel and the data channel in either order. A signal channel session is not active until the agents have agreed on parameters such as signal loss, mitigation lifetime and heartbeat intervals.

Both sides send periodic heartbeats so that an idle channel can be told apart from a dead one. Operators SHOULD set the heartbeat interval so it does not cause accidental denial of service. Either side may consider the session terminated after an extended absence of its peer's heartbeat.
sections.plainLanguage: The two sides keep saying "still here?" and "still here!" to each other. If one side goes quiet for too long, the other decides the line is dead.

sections.title: Modes of Signaling
sections.content:
The RFC describes several ways signaling can be arranged:

  • Direct: client and server talk straight to each other, inside or between domains.
  • Redirected: a server hands a client to another server, for example when it has reached its maximum number of sessions, its mitigator is out of capacity or down, or maintenance is scheduled.
  • Recursive: a mitigating domain that is overwhelmed acts as a client itself and asks a separate domain's DOTS server for help. This is opaque to the original client, though the recursing domain SHOULD pass back feedback.
  • Anycast: servers share an anycast service address. This can simplify client configuration and add resilience, but a route change can send the client to a server that lacks its security state, which may make sessions and mitigations flap.

Network address translation also needs thought, because an attack seen behind a NAT targets internal addresses, which a mitigator cannot use. The RFC describes directly provisioned address mappings, Port Control Protocol, STUN and DNS names as ways to work out the public scope.
sections.plainLanguage: There are different ways to pass the message: call the helper directly, be told to call a different helper, have the helper call a bigger helper, or dial one shared number that reaches whoever is nearest.

sections.title: Triggering a Mitigation Request
sections.content:
The architecture does not say when a client should ask for mitigation; that is up to the operator. It describes three styles of trigger.

A manual request is prepared or chosen by an operator, perhaps after an email, phone call or monitoring alert. An automated conditional request fires when operator-set conditions are met, such as a packet rate or byte rate being exceeded, resource exhaustion, or a count of connections or attack sources. An automated mitigation on loss of signal request starts only when the server stops receiving client heartbeats beyond the permitted miss count or interval.

The loss-of-signal option needs caution. Signal can be lost for reasons other than an attack, so mitigating on that basis may cost money and hurt network performance without need.
sections.plainLanguage: You can press the alarm button yourself, set the alarm to go off when the crowd gets too big, or tell the guards to come if you ever stop answering the phone. That last one might send guards for no reason if the phone just broke.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC names three primary attack vectors: agent impersonation, traffic injection and signal blocking. An attacker who can impersonate an agent or inject messages could trigger or cancel traffic redirection and mitigation, or subvert drop-lists and accept-lists.

DOTS agents MUST perform mutual authentication, and servers MUST verify that a client is authorized to request mitigation for the specific target resources. Received data may include topology, telemetry and mitigation details, so it SHOULD be protected at rest according to local policy. DOTS servers MUST be given adequate protection per best current practice, because an attack on server availability can stop mitigation requests from being handled.

An attacker controlling a client could request and withdraw mitigation for particular prefixes, causing route or DNS flapping, so operators should monitor and audit clients. The document has no IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: Bad guys might pretend to be the shop, tell fake stories to the guards, or block the phone line. So everybody has to prove who they are, and the guards must check that the shop only asks about its own doors.
